content.study:
Topic at a Glance
Article 239B of the Constitution of India is titled “Power of administrator to promulgate Ordinances during recess of Legislature”. It forms an integral component of The Union Territories (Articles 239–242), located within the “Union Territories” cluster. Current through the 106th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2023.

Constitutional Text & Anatomy
(1) If at any time, except when the Legislature of the Union territory of Puducherry is in session, the administrator thereof is satisfied that circumstances exist which render it necessary for him to take immediate action, he may promulgate such Ordinances as the circumstances appear to him to require:

Provided that no such Ordinance shall be promulgated by the administrator except after obtaining instructions from the President in that behalf:

Provided further that whenever the said Legislature is dissolved, or its functioning remains suspended on account of any action taken under any such law as is referred to in clause (1) of article 239A, the administrator shall not promulgate any Ordinance during the period of such dissolution or suspension.

(2) An Ordinance promulgated under this article in pursuance of instructions from the President shall be deemed to be an Act of the Legislature of the Union territory which has been duly enacted after complying with the provisions in that behalf contained in any such law as is referred to in clause (1) of article 239A, but every such Ordinance—

(a) shall be laid before the Legislature of the Union territory and shall cease to operate at the expiration of six weeks from the reassembly of the Legislature or if, before the expiration of that period, a resolution disapproving it is passed by the Legislature, upon the passing of the resolution; and

(b) may be withdrawn at any time by the administrator after obtaining instructions from the President in that behalf.

(3) If and so far as an Ordinance under this article makes any provision which would not be valid if enacted in an Act of the Legislature of the Union territory referred to in clause (1) article 239A" . Constituent Assembly Intent & Doctrinal Foundation
The framers envisioned Article 239B as a fundamental structural instrument. In constitutional jurisprudence, every clause operates not in isolation but as part of an integrated, transformative organic document. It regulates executive, legislative, or fundamental citizen interests to maintain the rule of law and constitutional supremacy.

Procedural & Courtroom Anchors (Senior Counsel Checklist)
1. Competent Forum: High Court under Article 226 (judicial review of legislative and executive action, challenge to vires) and Supreme Court under Article 136 (Special Leave Petition) / Article 32 (if fundamental rights are violated).
2. Standard of Review: Ultra vires doctrine, legislative competence (Lists I, II, III of Seventh Schedule), non-arbitrariness under Article 14, and procedural vires.
3. Standing & Remedial Path: Aggrieved party whose legal, statutory, or constitutional rights are infringed, or public-spirited person in representative actions where public interest is directly affected.
4. Evidentiary Standards: Where disputed facts or legislative arbitrariness are alleged, evidentiary burdens under the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA ss. 104–106) and official gazette notifications govern the record.

Key Statutory Ingredients to Establish
1. (1) If at any time, except when the Legislature of the Union territory of Puducherry is in session, the administrator thereof is satisfied that circumstances exist which render it necessary for him to take immediate action, he may promulgate such Ordinances as the circumstances appear to him to require:
2. Provided that no such Ordinance shall be promulgated by the administrator except after obtaining instructions from the President in that behalf:
3. Provided further that whenever the said Legislature is dissolved, or its functioning remains suspended on account of any action taken under any such law as is referred to in clause (1) of article 239A, the administrator shall not promulgate any Ordinance during the period of such dissolution or suspension.
4. (2) An Ordinance promulgated under this article in pursuance of instructions from the President shall be deemed to be an Act of the Legislature of the Union territory which has been duly enacted after complying with the provisions in that behalf contained in any such law as is referred to in clause (1) of article 239A, but every such Ordinance—
5. (a) shall be laid before the Legislature of the Union territory and shall cease to operate at the expiration of six weeks from the reassembly of the Legislature or if, before the expiration of that period, a resolution disapproving it is passed by the Legislature, upon the passing of the resolution; and
6. (b) may be withdrawn at any time by the administrator after obtaining instructions from the President in that behalf.

Judicial Interpretation & Binding Ratios
1. Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973) (1973) 4 SCC 225: The Constitution is the supreme law of the land; constitutional provisions must be harmoniously construed to preserve its basic structure and core institutional balance.
2. Minerva Mills Ltd. v. Union of India (1980) (1980) 3 SCC 625: Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles form the bedrock of the Constitution; institutional boundaries and constitutional discipline cannot be breached.

Current-Law Position & Milestone
Current through the 106th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2023. Any attempt by subordinate legislation or executive notifications to abridge the mandate of Article 239B is subject to judicial review under Articles 226 and 32.

I. ISSUE & CONSTITUTIONAL CONTEXT
Whether the State action, statutory enactment, or individual claim conforms to the constitutional mandate, procedural prerequisites, and substantive protections enshrined in Article 239B (Power of administrator to promulgate Ordinances during recess of Legislature) of the Constitution of India.

II. RULE & STATUTORY ANATOMY
Article 239B is situated in The Union Territories (Articles 239–242), governing the “Union Territories” dimension of Indian constitutional law.
The essential constitutional ingredients are:
1. (1) If at any time, except when the Legislature of the Union territory of Puducherry is in session, the administrator thereof is satisfied that circumstances exist which render it necessary for him to take immediate action, he may promulgate such Ordinances as the circumstances appear to him to require:
2. Provided that no such Ordinance shall be promulgated by the administrator except after obtaining instructions from the President in that behalf:
3. Provided further that whenever the said Legislature is dissolved, or its functioning remains suspended on account of any action taken under any such law as is referred to in clause (1) of article 239A, the administrator shall not promulgate any Ordinance during the period of such dissolution or suspension.
4. (2) An Ordinance promulgated under this article in pursuance of instructions from the President shall be deemed to be an Act of the Legislature of the Union territory which has been duly enacted after complying with the provisions in that behalf contained in any such law as is referred to in clause (1) of article 239A, but every such Ordinance—
5. (a) shall be laid before the Legislature of the Union territory and shall cease to operate at the expiration of six weeks from the reassembly of the Legislature or if, before the expiration of that period, a resolution disapproving it is passed by the Legislature, upon the passing of the resolution; and
6. (b) may be withdrawn at any time by the administrator after obtaining instructions from the President in that behalf.

III. PROCEDURAL ANCHOR & REMEDIAL FORUM
1. Competent Forum: High Court under Article 226 (judicial review of legislative and executive action, challenge to vires) and Supreme Court under Article 136 (Special Leave Petition) / Article 32 (if fundamental rights are violated).
2. Standard of Review: Ultra vires doctrine, legislative competence (Lists I, II, III of Seventh Schedule), non-arbitrariness under Article 14, and procedural vires.
3. Standing: Aggrieved party whose legal, statutory, or constitutional rights are infringed, or public-spirited person in representative actions where public interest is directly affected.

IV. JUDICIAL INTERPRETATION & AUTHORITY
In Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973) (1973) 4 SCC 225, the Supreme Court established that The Constitution is the supreme law of the land; constitutional provisions must be harmoniously construed to preserve its basic structure and core institutional balance.
Furthermore, in Minerva Mills Ltd. v. Union of India (1980) (1980) 3 SCC 625, the Court reaffirmed that constitutional guarantees are justiciable and binding upon all state functionaries.

V. APPLICATION TO FACT PATTERNS
To apply Article 239B:
1. Verify whether the impugned measure falls within the scope of the article's textual command.
2. Check whether any express exceptions, provisos, or constitutional limitations apply.
3. Subject the measure to tests of proportionality and non-arbitrariness under Article 14. If an ingredient is missing or breached, the measure is unconstitutional.

VI. CONCLUSION
Article 239B stands as a vital constitutional checkpoint. Any state action in breach thereof is void and amenable to writ jurisdiction under Articles 32 and 226. Current through the 106th Amendment (2023).

questionsAndAnswers.answer:
I. INTRODUCTION & CONSTITUTIONAL PHILOSOPHY
Article 239B of the Constitution of India, titled “Power of administrator to promulgate Ordinances during recess of Legislature”, represents a critical cornerstone of India’s constitutional democracy. Situated within The Union Territories (Articles 239–242), the provision balances state power with individual liberties and institutional accountability. The Constituent Assembly intended this provision to be an active, living guarantee rather than an ornamental declaration.
II. STATUTORY & DOCTRINAL DECONSTRUCTION
A forensic analysis of Article 239B reveals the following distinct constitutional limbs:
(a) Limb 1: (1) If at any time, except when the Legislature of the Union territory of Puducherry is in session, the administrator thereof is satisfied that circumstances exist which render it necessary for him to take immediate action, he may promulgate such Ordinances as the circumstances appear to him to require:
(a) Limb 2: Provided that no such Ordinance shall be promulgated by the administrator except after obtaining instructions from the President in that behalf:
(a) Limb 3: Provided further that whenever the said Legislature is dissolved, or its functioning remains suspended on account of any action taken under any such law as is referred to in clause (1) of article 239A, the administrator shall not promulgate any Ordinance during the period of such dissolution or suspension.
(a) Limb 4: (2) An Ordinance promulgated under this article in pursuance of instructions from the President shall be deemed to be an Act of the Legislature of the Union territory which has been duly enacted after complying with the provisions in that behalf contained in any such law as is referred to in clause (1) of article 239A, but every such Ordinance—
(a) Limb 5: (a) shall be laid before the Legislature of the Union territory and shall cease to operate at the expiration of six weeks from the reassembly of the Legislature or if, before the expiration of that period, a resolution disapproving it is passed by the Legislature, upon the passing of the resolution; and
(a) Limb 6: (b) may be withdrawn at any time by the administrator after obtaining instructions from the President in that behalf.
The Article must be read in conjunction with the foundational architecture of the Constitution:
1. Separation of Powers & Checks and Balances: No branch of government possesses untrammelled discretion.
2. Rule of Law & Non-Arbitrariness: Every exercise of authority under Article 239B must satisfy the basic standard of fairness and reasonableness.
3. Transformative Constitutionalism: The provision must be interpreted progressively to advance justice, liberty, and equality as pledged in the Preamble.
III. JURISPRUDENTIAL EVOLUTION & LEADING CASE LAW
The Supreme Court of India has deconstructed Article 239B across several seminal judgments:
1. Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973) (1973) 4 SCC 225:
   Ratio Decidendi: The Constitution is the supreme law of the land; constitutional provisions must be harmoniously construed to preserve its basic structure and core institutional balance.
2. Minerva Mills Ltd. v. Union of India (1980) (1980) 3 SCC 625:
   Ratio Decidendi: Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles form the bedrock of the Constitution; institutional boundaries and constitutional discipline cannot be breached.
IV. PROCEDURAL ROADMAP & LITIGATION CHECKLIST (SENIOR COUNSEL REFERENCE)
When approaching the Court under or in respect of Article 239B:
1. Forum Selection: High Court under Article 226 (judicial review of legislative and executive action, challenge to vires) and Supreme Court under Article 136 (Special Leave Petition) / Article 32 (if fundamental rights are violated).
2. Pleading Essentials: The writ petition or plaint must specifically plead:
   (a) The exact constitutional authority or violation under Article 239B;
   (b) The factual narrative establishing how each statutory ingredient is satisfied or infringed;
   (c) The absence of an effective alternative remedy, or justification under the Whirlpool Corporation exceptions (breach of fundamental rights, violation of natural justice, or complete lack of jurisdiction).
3. Evidentiary Standard: Discharge of burden under BSA ss. 104–106 and production of certified records.
V. IRAC PROBLEM ANALYSIS (PRACTICE HYPOTHETICAL)
Fact Matrix: The State issues a notification encroaching upon the domain of Article 239B without satisfying statutory preconditions.
Issue: Does the executive notification violate the constitutional guarantees and procedures of Article 239B?
Rule: Under Article 239B, state action is strictly conditioned by constitutional provisions and cannot be exercised arbitrarily.
Application: The impugned notification fails because it circumvents the procedural safeguards and lacks rational nexus to the constitutional objective. Applying the proportionality test, the State has failed to adopt the least intrusive means.
Conclusion: The notification is unconstitutional and void ab initio. The appropriate writ of certiorari or mandamus shall issue.
VI. CRITICAL APPRAISAL & CURRENT-LAW MILESTONE
Article 239B remains a vibrant instrument of governance, current through the 106th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2023. A robust democracy requires rigorous adherence to its letter and spirit to protect the citizen against executive overreach and legislative excesses.

### Constituent Intent & Doctrinal Evolution
The framers envisioned Article 239B as a fundamental structural instrument. In constitutional jurisprudence, every clause operates not in isolation but as part of an integrated, transformative organic document. It regulates executive, legislative, or fundamental citizen interests to maintain the rule of law and constitutional supremacy.

### Operational Mechanics & Judicial Standards
In practice, ARTICLE 239B functions as a direct constitutional parameter binding executive and legislative action. The Supreme Court of India has consistently held that powers exercised under this provision are not unfettered; they must comply with the overarching constitutional discipline of the Rule of Law, Article 14 non-arbitrariness, and the basic features of the Constitution. Aggrieved parties may invoke the writ jurisdiction of the High Courts under Article 226 or the Supreme Court under Article 32 to challenge actions that transgress the constitutional boundaries of this article.
